title: What do you do with your own bounce counts?
description: The bounce activity is tried again with your own counts for seven or more attempts. The board uses sample counts to show how to add them, divide by the number of attempts, and check the answer.
teaching_notes: One idea: with your own data, write every count, add them, and divide by the number of attempts you made. Watch for students who divide by seven even when they made more attempts.

video_script.why: The child has found an average from given counts and now has to collect counts and do the same.
video_script.substitution: Your own counts replace the given counts, and the number of attempts you made replaces eight.
video_script.anchor: A ball bounced on a bat and a notebook with a count for each of seven attempts
video_script.payoff_line: The sample average is six bounces per attempt

final_answer.value: Sample data 4, 7, 5, 9, 6, 3, 8 gives a mean of 6 bounces; your own answer depends on your data
final_answer.spoken: the sample data gives a mean of six bounces, and your own answer depends on your data

maths_rules: your own data: 7 or more attempts, so the divisor is the number of attempts you made
average = total / number of attempts = 42 / 7 = 6 bounces
video_script.design: A notebook page with seven sample counts. The board adds them, shares the total over the attempts, and multiplies back. A note says the divisor is always the number of attempts made.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; a ball bounces on a bat beside an empty notebook page with seven rows

marks.m1: the title card From your book appears
marks.m2: the ball bounces on the bat
marks.m3: the notebook page with seven empty rows appears
marks.m4: a question mark rises over the notebook

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>It asks you to try the bat and ball activity on your own.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>You count the bounces for seven or more attempts.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>What will you do with your counts to find their average?

beats.on_screen: the notebook stays on the board while the child thinks

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child who is thinking

beats.on_screen: the notebook rows fill with sample counts and carry the label sample data

marks.g1: the seven rows fill with sample counts
marks.g2: the label sample data appears on the notebook

narration: <bookmark mark='g1'/>Your counts will be your own.
<bookmark mark='g2'/>Here we use sample data to show the steps, the same way as the example in your book.

marks.given: the seven sample counts are written in a row

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the sample bounces in seven attempts are four, seven, five, nine, six, three and eight.

beats.on_screen: To find: the average number of bounces
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the average number of bounces.

marks.s1: the seven counts are added one after another

narration: <bookmark mark='s1'/>Step one, add all the counts to get the total.
<bookmark mark='s2'/>Four plus seven plus five plus nine plus six plus three plus eight makes forty two.

beats.on_screen: Step 2, average = total ÷ number of attempts: 42 ÷ 7 = 6

marks.d1: the rule average = total ÷ number of attempts is written

narration: <bookmark mark='d1'/>Step two, divide the total by the number of attempts.
<bookmark mark='d2'/>Forty two divided by seven gives six.

beats.on_screen: Step 3, check: 6 × 7 = 42, the same as the total; with your own data divide by the number of attempts you made

marks.c1: the 6 is repeated across the 7 attempts
marks.c2: the product 42 is matched with the total

narration: <bookmark mark='c1'/>Step three, check by putting the answer back.
<bookmark mark='c2'/>Six multiplied by seven is forty two, which is the total.
With your own counts, divide by the number of attempts you made.

beats.on_screen: Answer: sample data 4, 7, 5, 9, 6, 3, 8 gives a mean of 6 bounces; your own answer depends on your data
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The sample average is six bounces per attempt.
Your own answer will depend on your own data.
